newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada initials fur trapping pact with EU.
newsitem.headline: Canada initials fur trapping pact with EU.

text.p: Canada and the European Union have initialed an agreement on humane trapping standards, Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton said on Monday.
"It is an important step toward an eventual agreement," Eggleton said in a statement.

He said the pact would commit Canada and the EU to strict standards for trapping animals for pest control, conservation, fur and food and added: "I seriously urge the EU to approve this agreement as quickly as possible."
Russia was also expected to initial the agreement soon, he said.
The initialing of the agreement followed five months of intense talks. The European Commission told Canada and Russia in December to improve a draft agreement to ban leg-hold trapping.
Canada has made adjustments and now expects Europe to approve the agreement at meetings in June.
"We've gone the extra mile to try and accommodate their concerns," Canada's Foreign Affairs spokesman Charles Larabie said in a telephone interview.
"Every indication we've had is that we've now satisfied the demands that they had and I think we're on the road to seeing this thing resolved once and for all," Larabie said.

The adjustments strengthen Canada's commitment to ban leg-hold trapping, clarify the use of traditional traps by aboriginal people, increase the number of wild animals covered to 19 from 18 and make rulings of an arbitration body binding, the Canadian government said.
The proposed deal covers trapping of muskrats, beavers, sable, lynx, wolves and others. The time frame for compliance was also shortened, Larabie said.

Last December, EU environment ministers threatened to impose an import ban on fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps unless Canada, Russia and the United States accepted more humane trapping standards. Such a ban would have seriously harmed Canada's fur industry.
If the ministers sign the initialed agreement with Canada in June, it would end any threat of a ban, Larabie said.

Canada's fur industry employs about 100,000 people, about 80,000 of them trappers, of whom half are aboriginal. The industry in Canada generates about C$600 million ($436 million) in economic activity every year, the government said.
The European Union is the biggest customer for Canada's fur industry.
